hazards.food-drink-in-zone-decoy: That coffee cup is sitting inside the restricted area. Nothing gets eaten, drunk, or set down open inside a zone that might still carry contamination — it comes out of the area before the response continues, not after someone almost picks it back up.
hazards.paper-towel-decoy: That's an ordinary roll of paper towels sitting right by the spill. Paper towels don't absorb a hazardous drug spill the way the kit's own pads do, and pushing a spill around with the wrong material just spreads the contaminated area wider.
hazards.regular-trash-decoy: That's the regular trash bin, sitting closer than the hazardous-drug waste container. Anything that touched this spill goes into the dedicated stream — dropping it in whatever bin happens to be nearest turns ordinary trash into hazardous waste nobody downstream is expecting.
hazards.wrong-glove-grade-decoy: Those are ordinary exam gloves, not the kit's chemo-rated pair. A hazardous drug can permeate an exam glove in a way it can't get through the glove this kit was actually stocked with — the right pair is right next to the wrong one for a reason.

interrupts.alert: Once you start absorbing, the spill turns out to have spread further than it first looked — past what this kit is actually rated for.
interrupts.cue: This kit doesn't stretch to cover a bigger spill than it's built for.
interrupts.missNote: The response kept going with an undersized kit stretched past its rating. Whatever the kit ran out of partway through is still sitting there, uncontained.
interrupts.why: A kit rated for a certain size doesn't get pushed past that rating by using more of it than it's supposed to hold — a spill that turns out to be bigger gets escalated to the larger response this facility has for exactly that situation, not absorbed with a kit that's already running short.
interrupts.wrongNote: Call for the larger response — this kit was never rated to cover a spill this size.

interrupts.alert: A coworker walks up and leans on the counter right at the edge of the restricted zone, unaware anything happened here.
interrupts.cue: The barrier only works if it's actually enforced.
interrupts.missNote: The coworker stayed leaned against the counter, right at the edge of a zone that was supposed to be kept clear. The barrier existed on the floor but not in practice.
interrupts.why: A restricted zone that people wander up to unchallenged isn't actually restricted — reinforcing the barrier the moment someone gets close is what keeps the whole response's containment meaningful all the way through, not just at the moment it was first set up.
interrupts.wrongNote: Reinforce the barrier — a restricted zone nobody enforces isn't actually restricted.

lateNotes.log-incident: Not yet — the kit gets restocked before this incident is ready to close out.
lateNotes.restock-spill-kit: Hold that. The final decon wipe hasn't been done yet.
lateNotes.spill-waste-bag: Nothing sealed and ready yet — the waste has to actually be bagged first.

name: Hazardous Drug Spill Kit Response

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the spilled item's safety data sheet before doing anything else.
steps.prompt: Check the spilled item's safety data sheet before doing anything else.
steps.title: Identify the spill against its own SDS
steps.why: The SDS is what tells you this is actually a hazardous drug and not something else that happens to look similar — responding to a spill without checking what it actually is means guessing at every decision that follows, from what PPE this calls for to which waste stream it eventually goes in.

steps.cue: Set up barriers and keep everyone clear of the spill before PPE even comes out.
steps.prompt: Set up barriers and keep everyone clear of the spill before PPE even comes out.
steps.title: Restrict the area before anyone gets close
steps.why: A spill nobody's cordoned off is a spill anyone can walk through, touch, or track further down the hallway without ever knowing it happened — the barrier goes up before the response starts, not once someone's already wandered through the area and carried part of it somewhere else.

steps.cue: Gown first, then double-glove over the cuffs, then respiratory protection if the spill calls for it.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Gown, then gloves over the cuffs, then respiratory protection — that order is what keeps the gap at your wrist from ever opening.
steps.prompt: Gown first, then double-glove over the cuffs, then respiratory protection if the spill calls for it.
steps.title: Don PPE in the order that protects you
steps.why: USP <800> treats hazardous-drug PPE as a set donned in a specific order for a reason — a gown after gloves leaves a gap at the wrist, and respiratory protection last means it's the one thing you're not tempted to touch again once your gloved hands have already been near the spill.

steps.cue: Assess the spill's size and confirm it's within what this kit is actually rated to handle.

gauge.label: SPILL SIZE
gauge.missNote: Committed on a spill you never actually confirmed was within this kit's rating. A spill that size needs the larger response, not a guess that this kit will stretch to cover it.

steps.prompt: Assess the spill's size and confirm it's within what this kit is actually rated to handle.
steps.title: Read the spill against the kit's rated capacity
steps.why: Every spill kit is rated for a maximum size in its own instructions — committing to clean up a spill bigger than that rating with a kit that isn't built for it just means running out of absorbent mid-response with contamination still spreading.

steps.cue: Lay the kit's absorbent pads over the spill from the outside edge in.
steps.prompt: Lay the kit's absorbent pads over the spill from the outside edge in.
steps.title: Absorb the spill with the kit's own pads
steps.why: Working from the outside edge in is what keeps the contaminated area from spreading further while it's being absorbed — the kit's own pads are rated for this exact chemistry in a way a generic paper product never is.

steps.cue: Use the kit's small scoop and forceps to collect broken glass or vial fragments — never by hand.
steps.prompt: Use the kit's small scoop and forceps to collect broken glass or vial fragments — never by hand.
steps.title: Collect any fragments with the kit's scoop
steps.why: A hazardous drug spill that includes broken glass is two hazards stacked in the same footprint — the scoop and forceps in the kit exist so no bare or gloved hand ever has to close around a fragment that's both sharp and contaminated at the same time, in the same motion.

steps.cue: Two things near this spill are still contaminated and easy to miss. Find them.

itemNames.contaminated-linen: linen that caught part of the spill
itemNames.satellite-droplets: a trail of smaller droplets leading away from the spill

itemNotes.contaminated-linen: That linen caught part of the spill before you even got here — it goes into the same hazardous-drug stream as everything else this response collects, not the regular laundry bin.
itemNotes.satellite-droplets: A trail of smaller droplets means this spill travelled further than the main puddle shows — the response isn't done until every one of them is found and absorbed, not just the part that was obvious from the doorway.

steps.prompt: Two things near this spill are still contaminated and easy to miss. Find them.
steps.title: Scan for where the spill actually reached
steps.why: A spill's visible edge is rarely its actual edge — this scan is what catches the linen it soaked into and the trail it left, because a response that stops at the obvious puddle can still leave real contamination sitting a few feet away, waiting for the next person who walks through unaware.

steps.cue: Place every absorbent pad, glove, and contaminated item into the hazardous-drug waste bag and seal it.
steps.prompt: Place every absorbent pad, glove, and contaminated item into the hazardous-drug waste bag and seal it.
steps.title: Seal everything into the hazardous-drug stream
steps.why: Every item this spill touched — pads, gloves, linen, the gown itself — belongs in one dedicated stream, sealed, because a hazardous-drug waste bag with a gap in what it actually contains isn't a contained spill, it's a contained puddle with contaminated items still sitting around it.

steps.cue: Wash the affected surface with detergent solution after the spill itself is fully absorbed.
steps.prompt: Wash the affected surface with detergent solution after the spill itself is fully absorbed.
steps.title: Clean the surface with detergent and water
steps.why: Absorbing the spill removes the bulk of it; the detergent wash is what actually breaks down whatever residue is left behind on the surface itself, which is a genuinely separate step from soaking up the liquid, not a shortcut that happens automatically once the puddle itself is gone.

steps.cue: Wipe the surface and keep steady, even pressure — not too light, not scrubbing hard enough to spread anything — for the label's full contact time.
steps.holdBreakNote: The wipe came off pressure before the label's contact time was up. A decon pass that stops early hasn't actually broken down what's left on the surface.
steps.prompt: Wipe the surface and keep steady, even pressure — not too light, not scrubbing hard enough to spread anything — for the label's full contact time.
steps.title: Hold the final decon wipe to its contact time
steps.why: The decontaminating solution's own label sets how long it has to stay in contact with the surface to actually work, and pressure matters too — too light and it barely touches the surface, too hard and you risk spreading residue instead of lifting it.

steps.cue: Carry the sealed waste bag to the dedicated hazardous-drug waste container, not the general or regulated one.

drag.missNote: Not in the hazardous-drug bin — this waste doesn't belong in general or regulated streams, only its own.

steps.prompt: Carry the sealed waste bag to the dedicated hazardous-drug waste container, not the general or regulated one.
steps.title: Move the sealed bag to the hazardous-drug bin
steps.why: The hazardous-drug bin is tracked and disposed of under its own rule, kept entirely separate from general and regulated medical waste — a bag that ends up in the wrong container is waste that gets handled under a rule that was never written for what it actually contains.

steps.cue: Turn the kit's restock indicator once every component is replaced.
steps.prompt: Turn the kit's restock indicator once every component is replaced.
steps.title: Restock the spill kit
steps.why: A spill kit that's been used and never restocked is a kit that looks perfectly ready sitting on its shelf and isn't — turning it back to ready is what makes sure the next spill, whenever and wherever it happens, finds a full kit waiting instead of an empty box with the label still facing out.

steps.cue: Outer gloves first, then the gown, then respiratory protection, then the inner gloves last.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Outer gloves, then gown, then respirator, then inner gloves last — that sequence is what keeps the most contaminated layer away from your skin the longest.
steps.prompt: Outer gloves first, then the gown, then respiratory protection, then the inner gloves last.
steps.title: Doff PPE in the order that keeps you clean
steps.why: The most contaminated layer comes off first and the layer closest to your bare skin comes off last — reverse that order and a hand that just touched the outside of a contaminated gown is the hand about to touch your own face on the way to removing a respirator.

steps.cue: Record what happened, the response taken, and that the area is cleared.
steps.prompt: Record what happened, the response taken, and that the area is cleared.
steps.title: Log the spill incident
steps.why: The log is what turns this response into something the facility can actually review — a pattern of spills in the same spot, a kit that keeps running short, a training gap — none of that is visible to anyone if this incident only exists as something you remember handling.

supportLine: your employer's employee assistance program, or SEIU-UHW's member resources if a spill like this one has you more rattled than the shift usually is
tagline: The area restricted first, PPE donned in order, the spill sized against the kit's own rated capacity, absorbed and collected with the kit's own tools, sealed into the hazardous-drug stream, decontaminated to the label's contact time, and logged
